title: The fish became more alike
hook: An antidepressant made these fish more alike.
paper_title: Psychoactive pollution suppresses individual differences in fish behaviour
citation: Polverino et al. (2021), Proc. R. Soc. B
summary: In a two-year experiment with replicated guppy populations, fluoxetine exposure reduced between-individual variation in activity without a clear treatment difference in mean activity. Variation in risk-taking did not show the same response.
evidence_note: Twelve mesocosm populations, four per treatment; individual fish were repeatedly tested. posts.caption:
TT-002-REEL | WHAT CAN AN AVERAGE HIDE?

A group can change even when its average looks similar. In a two-year experiment, researchers maintained guppies in 12 large tanks: four separate populations per treatment, with no, low or higher fluoxetine exposure. Fluoxetine is an antidepressant.

Repeated behavioural tests found less variation between individual fish in activity in exposed populations. Mean activity did not clearly differ between treatments.

The limit matters: variation in risk-taking did not show the same response. This is not evidence that every fish lost its personality, or that wild fish populations declined. Results can depend on the trait and exposure conditions.

Original research: Polverino et al. (2021), Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2020.2294
Research library: https://akshaymohan16.github.io/toxic-tales-library/#tt-002-the-average-can-hide

Reference guppy imagery: 5snake5, CC0. Original explanatory animations and synthetic narration; not experimental footage. Follow @toxic_tales_eco for the science behind the story.

#ToxicTales #Ecotoxicology #FishBehaviour #FreshwaterEcology #ScienceCommunication

TT-002-CAROUSEL | BEHIND THE STUDY: AVERAGES AND INDIVIDUALS

The average is not the whole story. This companion to TT-002 separates the treatment comparison, repeated measurements and study limits.

Twelve independent guppy populations provided four tanks per treatment. Of 180 sampled fish, 174 completed all four behavioural trials. Fish were subsamples within exposure tanks, not 174 independent dose replicates.

The reported change was reduced between-individual activity variation, without a clear treatment difference in mean activity. Risk-taking variation did not show that same response. A non-significant mean difference is not proof that the true means are identical.

This two-year mesocosm result cannot establish the loss of all personality traits or a decline of wild populations.

Polverino et al. (2021), Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2020.2294

slides.headline: THE AVERAGE IS NOT THE WHOLE STORY
slides.body: Behind TT-002: a guppy experiment examined both the average activity of a population and the differences between individual fish.

slides.headline: WHAT WAS REPLICATED?
slides.body: Twelve large exposure tanks: four independent populations per treatment. Fish received no, low or higher fluoxetine exposure over two years.

slides.headline: REPEATED FISH, NOT EXTRA TANKS
slides.body: Of 180 sampled fish, 174 completed all four behavioural trials. Those repeated tests revealed individual differences. They did not create 174 independent exposure tanks.

slides.headline: WHAT DID THE AVERAGE SHOW?
slides.body: Mean activity did not clearly differ between treatments. A non-significant difference does not prove that the true means are identical.

slides.headline: WHAT DID INDIVIDUALS REVEAL?
slides.body: Between-individual variation in activity was lower in exposed populations. Risk-taking variation did not show the same pattern. One behavioural trait is not an animal's entire personality.

slides.headline: WHAT REMAINS UNPROVEN?
slides.body: The study did not demonstrate wild-population decline or show that the effects were permanent. Findings can depend on the trait, species and exposure conditions.

slides.headline: FOLLOW THE EVIDENCE
slides.body: Read the original study and the limits in our research library. DOI: 10.1098/rspb.2020.2294. Follow @toxic_tales_eco for research-backed stories.

evidence.design: Two years; 12 mesocosm populations, four per treatment. Repeated tests of individual fish; fish are subsamples, tanks are exposure replicates. Measured fluoxetine approximately 40 and 366 ng/L.

claims.claim: Exposed populations showed lower between-individual activity variation.
Mean activity showed no clear treatment difference.
claims.location: Results 3(a), treatment effect p=0.275; not an equivalence test.

claims.claim: Risk-taking variation did not show the same response.
174 fish completed all four repeated behavioural trials.
claims.location: Methods 2(c), repeated behavioural assays; 180 sampled initially.

limitations: Activity is one trait, not all personality.
Experimental populations do not establish wild population decline.
A non-significant mean comparison does not prove identical means.

segments.speech: An antidepressant made these fish more alike.
Not in appearance. In how active they were.
Researchers raised guppy populations for two years, across twelve tanks: four per treatment.
Then they tested individual fish repeatedly.
With fluoxetine exposure, activity differed less from fish to fish. Yet average activity showed no clear difference.
That is a change an average alone could miss.
But risk-taking did not show the same pattern. This experiment did not demonstrate declining wild populations.
The lesson? Look beyond the average. Real science. Dark twists. Follow Toxic Tales.
